Nowhere to Hide BY JOE FORDHAM narrative follows two British Army soldiers - 8th Battalion London Regiment Lance Corporals George Schofield (George MacKay) and Tom Blake (Dean-Charles Chapman) - entrusted to deliver a message from General Erinmore (Colin Firth) to an associate behind enemy lines. Nine miles away, Colonel Mackenzie (Benedict Cumberbatch), commander of 2nd Battalion Devonshire Regiment, is planning an attack that aerial intelligence has revealed will lead them into an enemy trap. With wire communications severed, it is up to Blake and Schofield to halt the attack, potentially saving the lives of 1,600 men, including Blake's elder brother. for best visual effects, was characterized by a gambit that Mendes made clear in a preface to the screenplay, stating that the story was to be told in real time, and - with the exception of one moment - in a single continuous shot. Ihe concept for Universal Pictures' World War I drama, 1917, was simple. As crafted by director Sam Mendes and co-screenwriter Krysty Wilson-Cairns, the The deceptively simple storyline of the movie, which went on to earn the 2020 Oscar 1 / 31 To investigate the Hitchcockian premise - first attempted in the master of sus-

pense's 1948 Rope, and more recently seen in Alejandro Iñarritu's Birdman - Mendes 1917 gathered close collaborators, including cinematographer Roger Deakins and production designer Dennis Gassner, for a lengthy preproduction. "From Day One," noted visual effects producer Sona Pak, the 'single shot' concept was part of the story. It was not a gimmick. The camera wasn't ever allowed to see or go anywhere that the two characters weren't going. We never had a wide view, craning up or traveling where the boys weren't going. They were committed to that idea, but they never compromised shooting techniques for the one-shot concept." Planning involved six months of storyboarding, set design, location scouting and rehearsals. Mendes and Deakins began blocking scenes at Shepperton Studios and at locations, using tape markers, poles and cones to delineate camera and performer paths. "Roger and Sam marked out the length of each shot where we planned to shoot," Pak explained. As they paced out scenes with the actors, they tried different camera rigs, walking through scenes with camera operators. Sam sometimes edited the script to fit dialogue to distances that the actors had to travel, and he occasionally re-designed sets to help the camera rigs. The art department gave us set plans and schematics, showing where the boys and the camera traveled. They designed every shot to ensure they weren't ever compromising how Sam wanted to tell the story. It was an intimate journey, focused on our two guys, and it involved a very thoughtful and disciplined approachi To re-create battlefields of war-torn Northern France, many of which still contain the unmarked remains of an estimated 20 million personnel killed in action, the film2 / 31 makers wove together a tapestry of rural English settings. Dennis Gassner's team trans-

formed expanses of Salisbury Plain, in Wiltshire, and Bovingdon Airfield, in Hertfordshire, into trenches and No Man's Land. Special effects worked with art department and camera teams to re-create unimaginably harsh battle conditions where soldiers huddled in wooden trenches in sodden, freezing mud.iWe added water at the last possible moment and monitored that on a daily basis," noted special effects supervisor Dominic Tuohy. "We analyzed water samples for bacteria, or Weil's disease, and constantly replaced the set with fresh water. It was on a very large scale, especially with the camera going through trenches and into No Man's Land, where everything was sodden, and in real clay mud. designer Tristan Versluis.We were all very sensitive to the research that the production team had brought together with their historical advisors. We knew we had to be mindful of the amount of life that was lost and the circumstances of the soldiers' deaths in our prosthetic work. Sam didn't want the gore and horror to be in the audience's face, but it had to be there as part of the atmosphere and landscape. Bodies were left out in No Man's Land to rot because no one could retrieve them at night. And there were many sad stories about the animals that died, particularly horses. Historical advisors Andrew Robertshaw and Peter Barton advised on details of trench warfare, hygiene and grooming, which Versluis' team re-created, in collaboration with makeup and hair designer Naomi Donne, in prosthetics and moustache hair pieces. For 1917 istorical reference revealed harrowing perspectives of carnage that the filmmakers strove to represent in prosthetic builds.iMy great-granddad was involved in both wars, and my granddad in the second,i remarked prosthetic 3 / 31

corpses, the production commissioned prosthetic bodies rather than makeup on perform1917 ers. "We made 30 hero dummies in varieties of decomposition, and some eaten by rats," said Versluis. 'The casting department provided us with actors who represented soldiers' faces accurate to the period. So many were just naive teenagers who signed up for this adventure with no idea what they were walking into. We wanted to capture that look of shocked innocence. We lifecast each person, made molds of heads and hands. From those, we produced Plastilina clay pours and then sculpted open eyes, wounds and extra detailing. We molded those and created silicone heads and hands that we painted and individually hair-punched. We jointed each body to make them flexible, so we could position them in realistic ways, and reused them in different scenesi Animal prosthetics included a dead dog and three horses. Versluis' team used Pixologic ZBrush to create a horse sculpture with interchangeable limbs, and right and left flanks that represented different levels of decomposition. Three-dimensional geometry was then output to a 3D milling machine, which generated a rigid foam master model. We created a horse design we could lay on one side to look bloated and then flip to reveal a cutaway belly in an emaciated version," explained Versluis. "We molded and cast that in Plastilina, sculpted extra detail around the eyes, nose and hooves, then molded and cast it in foam and silicone. We used electrostatic flocking to apply synthetic hair, shaping different fur directions, and hand-punched longer hairs. By modeling in 3D, we could show our design to Sam early on, for his approval." The exterior location shoot, with the roving camera taking in 360-degree views of 4 / 31 war-torn terrain, put extraordinary demands on the production. The camera team favored

1917 cloudy skies for visual continuity, and monitored camera feeds from tents long distances from shooting sites. To plan for days when the English spring weather was unnaturally sunny, the production scheduled weather coverage sets built in barns near main locations. "Any time we had bright sunlight," said Sona Pak, "we would spend the day rehearsing shots on that location. When the weather was right, we'd been through rehearsals in such detail everyone was ready to go, hitting their marks, getting what they needed. On average, we completed one setup a day. There were days where, if sunny weather prevented shooting the previous day, we shot two setups. It was a pretty fierce boot camp but it worked out in our favor. We were scheduled to shoot for 70 days, but we finished in 65." The production shot the majority of Schofield and Blake's journey in continuity, while editorial and visual effects teams oversaw assembly of the film concurrently in London. MPC provided connective tissue that blended takes into the single-shot illusion. To gauge the dovetailing of Shot 'A' into the beginning of Shot 'B,' on-set visual effects supervisor David Griffiths worked with a video assist team to review selected takes. Film editor Lee Smith then worked in his cutting room in Soho with a team of postvis artists from Cheap Shot VFX who overnight assembled mockups of digital stitches. The editorial team then relayed approvals back to set, giving Mendes the all clear to move on with the next section of his shoot. Meanwhile, MPC ingested footage and executed seamless blends. More complicated set pieces - including a sequence involving an encounter with a fallen canal bridge - required special planning, technical rehearsals and previsualization 5 / 31 from Proof. "We shot our canal sequence at Govan Graving Docks in Glasgow," related

Pak. We reviewed the location and what Sam wanted to shoot. Back at Shepperton, they built a replica on the backlot and marked out the distances of the canal. They worked out how they'd use multiple cranes to support George on a wire, as he walked over the downed bridge, and another two cranes to move the camera over the canal. They rehearsed that action, and worked out how George could unhook himself from the wire as he and the camera crossed the bridge. The camera operators then lifted the camera from its wire rig and continued to follow George as he reached the other side, all in one smooth take. They rehearsed that so thoroughly, when we went to Scotland for the location shoot, the two shots we were due to complete in four days, we finished in two. tions of gyro-stabilizing rigs - Steadicam, StabilEye, Trinity and Dragonfly - combined with cranes, cable winches, camera cars, ATVS and an aerial drone. Handoffs required a ballet of coordination between grip and camera teams. "As Schofield and Blake approached a crater in No Man's Land," said Pak, "the operator carried the camera and, on the move, grips mounted the camera to a four-point wire-cam setup. That rig then descended, followed the boys into the crater while the camera glided over water in the crater, and then rejoined them on the other side. We had a couple of scenes getting our characters in and out of trenches where we used cranes, but eighty percent of the shoot was handheld. Roger often operated, especially with the StabilEye, controlling camera 1917 o achieve unobtrusive, fluid-flowing shots traversing varieties of obstacles, Mendes and Deakins used multiple camera platforms with a trio of Arri Alexa Mini LFs. The compact and powerful prototype 4.5K cameras rode on combina6 / 31

1917 motion remotely from his tent." Deakins' team and first assistant director Michael Lerman choreographed beginning and end frames of each scene, aligning compositions via video assist. MPC then produced digital blends using mostly 2D compositing techniques.iThe stitches involved a lot of rotoscope and composite effects,i stated visual effects supervisor Greg Butler, who guided work at MPC Montréal, London and Bangalore. "The stitches were conceived and designed in preproduction and they incorporated those criteria into shot design. Conceptually, Sam didn't ever want the camera to drift away from the action in any distracted, dreamy way. Birdman did a lot of those transitions, very effectively, but they fit the nature of that film's dreamlike style. Sam wanted none of that. The other obvious stitch technique was the classic Rope trick, where the image went to black, facilitating a cut. In this movie, we had one time-cut, midway, when George loses consciousness. We had other scenes where the image went to black in a justified way - where the boys walk in or out of a dugout, or nighttime scenes where lighting momentarily went to black. But, in the latter, we purposely rotoscoped details and carried them through the stitch so, at no point, when the scene was viewed in a darkened cinema, was there a black frame. MPC created digital stitches with characters center frame using varieties of in-camera transition objects.®A transition object was anything that traveled through the scene as a moving mask that we used to leverage a stitch," Butler explained. "That gave the eye something to look at while we performed our sleight of hand. But in those moments, we wanted the camera to behave in a manner that felt natural. Occasionally, that technique 7 / 31 was convenient and worked dramatically in the context of a scene. Other times, it re-

sulted in much more complex stitches.i them toward what he dryly regards as their journey toward certain death. The transition occurred as the boys climb ramshackle wooden ladders, blending to a crane shot that ascends into a field of mud, corpses and barbed wire. Both pullback and crane moves were shot on location in Bovingdon Airfield. MPC bridged the hand-off between camera platforms. "It was the first week of shooting," Butler related. "There weren't many places to transition into No Man's Land, so they made the bold decision to do that stitch as they left the Sap Trench - that was the historical name, going back to Napoleonic times, for a trench that 'sappers' tunneled out from the Front Line to get past an area where there was no place to hide. That was a good analogy for us, too, as we had no place to hide. We had to stitch from the boys at the end of their camera run and get them up and over. They ended the A-side of the shot with the actors getting into position. When they came back for the continuation another day, the lighting was different. The actors did not re-create their exact positions and body postures. The camera didn't line up the same way. And, for whatever reason, the mud was not consistent on the boys' costumes. We aligned A- and B-sides of the stitch, slid them up and down. We did a slight re-speed to try to get, in particular, Blake to match to his A-side motion. But even when we aligned those elements, there was a section just before 1917 ne of the most complex stitches involved Schofield and Blake's exit from the Allied trenches into No Man's Land. The camera reverse-tracked with the characters as a shell-shocked Lieutenant Leslie (Andrew Scott) leads 8 / 31

1917 they went up that was so different, there was no way to converge A and B in an actor-toactor stitch. That's where we used a digi-double to make the plates connect. MPC CG supervisor Nick Sparks oversaw digi-double builds, while compositing supervisor Vijay Selvam and team in Bangalore extracted textures from plates to aid blends of performer faces, costumes, mud and weaponry. "We took what we could and used it," said Butler. "We decided that, although it was going to be hard, Blake could be reconstructed in 2D without a digi-double there. We were getting one ready but as the paint and prep team in Bangalore progressed, we saw promise in their work and we told them it was all on them. They took digital texture patches of Blake from the B-side plate, tracked them back into the A-side and created a 2D 'Frankenstein' of elements. By the time we transitioned, Blake became mostly his B-plate self. During the camera move, pushing forward with the boys, the A-side plate was a couple feet to the left of where the B-side camera continued. So, we also rebuilt the end of the Sap Trench, generated a virtual camera move and used that to bridge A- and B-cameras, transitioning between them. Schofield was even harder. He was the focus of the shot, and his action and the differences between the plates were too significant to save him in 2D. We used a digi-double there, but we limited that to only 18 pure digi-double frames. With a few frames either side, we created his animation to blend the plates togetheri With so much of the single-shot illusion riding on digital stitch techniques, the production laid out the rules of engagement in a Stitch Bible that Roger Deakins used to communicate with visual effects supervisor Guillaume Rocheron, who joined the team 9 / 31 as the film entered its postproduction phase. ¿The Stitch Bible evolved as we put the

movie together," said Rocheron. "Roger and Sam looked for places to do each stitch 1917 driven by how they needed to change the set and their camera rigs. Environment and camera stitches were more straightforward. Other times, during long takes, Sam occasionally decided he wanted to use a performance from one take and part of a performance from another. Those became unplanned stitches that were not decided on set. endes and editor Lee Smith shaped the film using more than five-dozen digM "On most visual effects films," Rocheron noted, "the production-side supervisor works hand in hand with editorial as the cut changes, scenes or shots are added, or eliminated. Here, that wasn't possible. Lee cut the movie while Sam was shooting. The only temporal alterations made in post were retimes. Using the Stitch Bible, we evaluated which transitions worked better than others, and we designed stitches that felt fluid. Roger's camera work was beautifully choreographed. It flowed naturally, and it never felt like the camera went anywhere to make a stitch work. That was the most important thing to consider in designing stitches. It was like a magic trick, and each transition had to land perfectly in a way that felt completely transparent. And then, all of our visual effects work had to be viewed not in 'shots,' but in the context of the movie. The film begins with Blake and Schofield resting by a tree as the camera rises and pulls back with the boys, summoned to meet Erinmore. As they enter a labyrinth of trenches, personnel carrying an ammunition crate briefly cross their path, right to left, 10 / 31 providing MPC compositing lead Suresh Pandi with the basis for the film's first digital

stitch. "The ammo box was one of our first stitches," recalled Greg Butler. "I naïvely 1917 thought: 'Oh, this one's going to be easy. We'll just roto the box, wipe from A to B, and do a little bit of correction.' But that work went on almost until the end of postproduction. Our first task was to align characters on the A- and B-sides of a stitch, beginning with their eyes because that was the focus of attention." MPC Bangalore used 2D tracking facilities in The Foundry Nuke to create alignments with 21⁄2D texture projections.Schofield was the focus of the shot. When we aligned his eyes across the stitch, we noticed Blake was off. When we corrected Blake's alignment, we noticed the trench wall was at different heights. When we corrected that, we noticed an actor in deep background was out of place. It was like pulling on a piece of thread - as soon as we got the basic building blocks of the actors and the foreground aligned, we were off elsewhere. The solution was to get the big pieces right, and then move to the medium, and then the smaller pieces, until we achieved the perfect stitch." Schofield and Blake receive their orders, ascend the Sap Trench and crawl through barbed wire into No Man's Land. Dennis Gassner's team dressed the field at Bovingdon to represent a desolate expanse of craters, broken tree stumps and barbed wire. Special effects supplied fencing sections with rubber-tipped barbs for performer interactions. Tristan Versluis' team added fallen corpses and a prosthetic wound for a gruesome detail when Schofield rips the palm of his hand. MPC revealed the wound using a subtle digital wipe on George MacKay's hand. Environment lead Jules Bodenstein and his team expanded the wasteland. "The first twoI1 / 31 thirds of No Man's Land were a large muddy set," said Butler. "The last third was digital.

Our first step there was to remove the distant tree line. The camera was low with the boys, so the horizon was clearly visible, showing green trees in the distance. That required a combination of intensive paintwork and roto through foreground poles and barbed wire. Working in 4K gave us a few more pixels to grab there. Our 3D environment department then extended the terrain with craters full of CG water and atmospheric treatments to obscure details out beyond a mile." MPC's 3D team added digital set dressing, including a derelict British Mark II tank, seen before the boys descend into a giant crater full of floating bodies. As the camera ascends the far side of the crater, Schofield reacts to a half-seen body suspended on barbed wire. "Originally there was a little bloodied tuft of hair in the wire," noted Butler. Sam and Lee decided Schofield's reaction to that was not fitting for a veteran of the Somme. We had our Schofield digi-double, so we did a version of the shot where Schofield saw his own corpse. We changed the corpse's face but, surprisingly, it was still recognizable as George. We had to change his ears, chin and hair so there was nothing left of him but his buzz-cuti sleeping quarters. As the characters use flashlights to explore the darkened living area, Blake discovers a large rat that scurries down to gnaw on a dangling food bag. Proof provided previs of the rat descending the bag. MPC Montréal animation supervisor Pascal 1917 chofield and Blake reach the German trenches and enter a deserted, heavily fortified enclave. The production built interiors, including a German bunkroom, in a Salisbury barn. MPC stitched from the battlefield location into the German 12 / 31

1917 Blais and animators Thibaud Chantrel and Shinoj Tj refined rodent performance.Our first criterion was to make sure the rat was big and mean enough," Butler recalled. "Sam stated these had to be evolutionary rats that were willing to do what other rats wouldn't do to survive, including standing up to soldiers taking potshots at them, so this had to be a particularly fat and nasty one. We had to determine how the rat met Blake's eyeline, how concerned it would be, reacting to the boys' lamps as it scurried across the roof beams. We animated a couple of takes on those relationships. Sam asked us to play the rat discreetly behind the food bag, revealing just its tail and a little bit of its face. We knew this movie was about the actors, the camera work and the environment; we didn't want the digital character to be distracting. But after a test screening, the audience had a big reaction to the rat, and Sam encouraged us to make it a more featured moment." The rat scurries toward a trip-wire in a doorway, a booby trap left by departing enemy troops, and a deafening explosion blasts Blake aside and buries Schofield under rubble. Special effects planned the blast and subsequent collapse, involving principal performers. "It was thoroughly choreographed and rehearsed," related Dominic Tuohy. "We planned to drop a beam with a designated stop-point. We then swung the beam out of shot to allow the cameraman to get through." Special effects initiated the explosion using a blast of CO2 with white powder. Visual effects stitched a whip-pan of Blake tugged backward. Rubble, dust and debris featured mixtures of practical organic materials. "If you can eat it, your body can absorb it," said Tuohy. We used food products and water-based materials for dust, and installed a big 13 / 31 extractor system. As soon as a take was over, we blasted fresh air through the set. We

1917 had to bury George, and Sam wanted the debris to look heavy. We made a floor section out of soft materials that we shaped around the actor, giving the impression there were rocks around him. We built lightweight debris that fitted together like a big jigsaw puzzle and then, for every take, replaced them the exact same way. We laid those on top of George, until only his mouth was exposed. At the last moment, we filled his mouth with coconut powder. We placed the last rocks over his head and they turned over camera. On action, we did an overlap of the CO2 blast so, as Blake dragged him up, there was dust raining down." ith the bunker collapsing, and Schofield blinded and spitting dust, Blake hauls his friend through an adjoining tunnel and they leap across an open mineshaft. The production placed a ramp across an opening in the floor, which the camera operator crossed. MPC digitally removed the ramp and added falling dust to in-camera effects. "The moment George gets pulled out of the rubble," noted Tuohy, "that's real dust. The moment they start through the corridor, that's real dust. When the camera was in front of the actors, looking back, we added dust behind them. But the moment the camera turned and followed them out, that's when we had a problem because we didn't want our dust to obscure camera. We dropped minimal dust there, with falling beams that we swung clear, and then visual effects added to those effects." Schofield and Blake emerge into a derelict artillery range littered with destroyed German field guns and 6,000 shell casings - shot in Ambrose Quarry in Oxfordshire. After 14 / 31 passing through trees into a field, the two young men spy a pair of biplanes. MPC mod-

1917 eled and animated the aircraft, and extended the aerial action into a dogfight that the boys view from an abandoned French farmhouse, a practical set constructed in a Salisbury meadow. The dogfight featured two British Sopwith Camels dueling with a German Albatros D.III, seen as tiny specks against the sky. Mendes used the barely seen aircraft to ratchet up the tension as the Albatros belches smoke, dips beneath a rise and then reemerges to slam into the barn. The aircraft crash relied on a blend of in-camera choreography, full-scale mechanical effects, and digital effects. We had to somehow get the CG plane in the air to suddenly hit the ground," related Guillaume Rocheron. "We had to do that from the boys' perspective and, without cutting, the actors had to rush forward to extract the pilot from the plane that had just crashed. It was a good example of our methodology, layering elements to create the most natural result.i Proof prevised the aircraft crash, which the filmmakers planned in three plates. The first had the two actors observing a drone in the sky, providing them and the camera operator with eyelines. The performers followed the drone's motion to the moment of impact, ducked and then ran toward the barn. For subsequent takes, set dressing and special effects teams redressed the location with a wrecked plane. The moment of impact featured a practical effect, which the special effects team staged using a re-creation of the German biplane against bluescreen.iMost of the film was shot in continuity except the plane crash element," noted Dominic Tuohy. "We took the building from the location in Salisbury, brought it back to Shepperton, replicated the 15 / 31 slope of the location, rebuilt the barn and installed a special rig that allowed us to move

1917 the plane down a track. The biggest challenge was to match the biplane's end position. We had the fuselage of the plane and one wing on our track, like a big Scalextric toy. We fired that from a nitrogen cannon at high speed, pulled it through the barn, which we rigged for a breakaway, and had a decelerator rig that stopped it. That gave us all the interaction with the ground and the dust; but as it went down the track, it turned, which gave us the movement we needed and mimicked the end position." MPC compositing lead Yuri Carrara used the practical crash element as the basis to reverse-engineer animation of the Albatros swooping in to impact, and bridged the stitch with a combination of practical effects and dynamic simulations of exploding timbers, dirt and pyrotechnics. "As the plane hit the barn," explained Guillaume Rocheron, "we generated digital destruction to blend to Dom's element. We then composited our crashing CO plane into the empty barn plate, and blended our animated plane into the practical crashed plane on locationi The multilayered stitch used action of Blake and Schofield ducking in fear and then moving forward, which MPC blended to the performers advancing to rescue the crashed German pilot (Robert Maaser). "As Schofield and Blake stand," said Rocheron, "the camera moved around them and we used that opportunity to do a stitch on their legs. We blended to a plate with the crashed plane on location. That prop then had to burn for the next seven minutes of screen time." "We piped in propane gas," Dominic Tuohy explained. "We rehearsed that thoroughly with the stuntman playing the pilot, and both main actors. When we turned over, we lit 16 / 31 the propane on the plane. The pilot had flammable liquid on his legs. As the boys ran

over and pulled him out, we waited until they lifted him up, and then ignited the pilot's legs so they were on fire as he came out. We knew the liquid on his legs would burn for 13 seconds so, and by the time they dropped him in the barnyard, the flames had been extinguished. That required a very strict regimen that everyone rigorously obeyed. And hats off to the actors because they were running in there while real flames were burning all around." was a huge scene," commented Tristan Versluis. "Naomi Donne created a death pallor makeup for Blake. We did a couple of tests to arrive at a level of paleness that Sam approved. We were tasked with creating a blood rig, as well. We knew there was nowhere to lay blood tubes in the ground, and we couldn't hide anywhere close to the performers because the camera was circling. My animatronic specialist, Pete Hawkins, did some research and found some little medical pumps used in surgery. They were small enough for the actor to wear and, with the correct gauge tubing, we built a prosthetic chest as a radio-controlled rig with blood pouches. It all fitted in Blake's webbing and the bags of his costume. Pete figured out how to make blood last by controlling the pump with a remote control transmitter. One of our biggest challenges was muffling the sound of the pump. We knew this was an emotional scene and we didn't want the motor going nerrr over Blake's last words. The boys' shock and subsequent struggle, turning slowly to despair, required 25 takes over two days, involving physical and digital effects and prosthetic sleight of hand.iIt 17 / 31

1917 sound guys to make it as soundproof as possiblei As Blake's life ebbs away, MPC supplied a subtle stitch to link two rotational camera moves that compositors orchestrated while leeching the lifeblood from the dying infantryman. A Stronger Loving World BY JOE FORDHAM In Alan Moore's 1988 afterword to his 1986 magnum opus, Watchmen - created with illustrator Dave Gibbons - the writer joked that he was done with promotions, done with talking about a movie adaptation, and generally done with superheroes. Moore's words were prophetic. Decades later, after a falling-out with publisher DC Comics, the maverick comic maven distanced himself from the material and, legend has it, skipped Zack Snyder's 2008 Watchmen feature film. When DC Films and HBO approached showrunner Damon Lindelof with the prospect of mounting a television series based on the Watchmen universe, it took some persuading. Lindelof was an acknowledged fan of the comic, which had turned stereotypes on their heads, and he innately sympathized with Moore's position as an author who had humanized costumed vigilantes, and then was dehumanized for his efforts. To quote the Roman poet: 'Who watches the Watchmen?' Instead of a remake or sequel, Lindelof proposed a kaleidoscopic remix of the Watchmen saga. The nine-part Watchmen mini-series revisited the meta-universe where 1 / 33 costumed crimefighters were an everyday fact of life and sprinkled in a brand new lineage

WATCHMEN of vigilantes, in multiple time periods, including a present-day resistance to a white supremacist cult, the Seventh Kavalry. Returning characters included arch villain Adrian Veidt (Jeremy Irons), one-time crimefighter now FBI agent Laurie Blake (Jean Smart), and Laurie's former lover, Jon Osterman, a scientist transformed after a laboratory accident into the omniscient superbeing, Dr. Manhattan (Yahya Abdul-Mateen II). Deep Waters BY JODY DUNCAN underwater, in the converted reactor containment building of an uncommissioned nuclear power plant in South Carolina. The underwater shoot was famously, even notoriously arduous for Cameron, cast and crew, but it gave the driven director in-camera shots of characters in deep water - shots that would have been impossible to achieve digitally, at a time when convincing water simulations were a thing of the future. Increased liability and safety concerns, as well as digital capabilities, led director William Eubank and the producing team at Chernin Entertainment to take a different approach for Underwater, about a crew at a mining operation site nearly seven miles below the ocean surface, forced to walk the seabed to another site when their station is irreparably damaged in a seismic event. The perilous journey is made more so when the characters are confronted by mysterious and predatory deep-sea creatures presumably disturbed by the drilling activities. The production plan, aided by previs from previs supervisor Michael Solorzano and 1 / 16 his crew at Proof, Inc., was to shoot the film's many underwater scenes dry-for-wet, on

UNDERWATER an all-black soundstage in New Orleans, into which special effects supervisor Mark Byers and his crew would pump smoke to create a murky, underwater look. Particulate and other features meant to sell the dry-for-wet plates as underwater environments would be added digitally by main vendor MPC. Eubank shot a 90-second proof-of-concept to sell the plan to 20th Century Fox executives, which earned Underwater its green light. For Eubank, the film's underwater environments would be as much a character in the story as Kristen Stewart's electrical engineer, Norah Price, and as threatening and scary as the deep-sea creatures. "Will wanted the film to be very claustrophobic," said production visual effects supervisor Blair Clark. "He wanted the audience to be in the dark, with only fleeting glimpses of things. Throughout the movie, Will wanted to tap into phobias - fear of the dark, fear of suffocation, fear of drowning, fear of closed spaces - and that influenced creature design, shot design, sets, everything." One of the complications of realizing the story's underwater setting was the fact that, at seven miles deep, the typical features of more shallow waters wouldn't be present to help sell the conceit. "It was so far down," said Clark, "it would be nothing but black, in reality, which made it a hard sell as an underwater environment. We realized early that if we went totally realistic with it, it would be a blank environment. There's nothing down there! It's crystal clear, there's no light to play off of, there's little or no sea life. So we had to take creative liberties with it. Luckily, storywise, it was established that there was this seismic event, and we took advantage of that to add a ton of particulate in postproduction to give us some movement and to sell the volume of the water." 2 / 16| To create floaty, underwater movements on the dry-for-wet stage, the actors per-

formed wide and mid-range shots on wire rigs designed and implemented by stunt coordinator Mark Rayner. For shots with no dialogue, the rigged performers were shot at 28 to 32 frames per second, which enhanced the underwater illusion. To suggest the characters' interaction with the underwater environment, special effects manipulated the set's sandy floor. "It was very difficult to get that dry environment to behave as if it was an underwater environment," noted Mark Byers. "There was sand and other materials on the floor of the stage, and we would move that to suggest characters were walking or a creature was going by. We disturbed the materials on the floor by slamming pneumatics into the ground. We built proxies of different shapes, depending on what we were trying to do, and we pushed those proxies into the silt to get it to move. And then, in postproduction, visual effects replaced the proxy." Kepler station, for example," said Byers, "they go into an elevator that sinks them down into the water. For that, we built a tank that was 20 by 20 feet, and eight feet deep, with an underwater elevator that lowered and raised the characters." Two additional stage tanks measured 20 by 40 feet, and one exterior tank was 80 feet long, ten feet wide, and six feet deep. This last was built especially for shots of characters running down a long corridor of the station as water rushes in from its breached walls. warm, treated, filtered water.iWe could pump that water into any one of the four tanks UNDERWATER for different sets," said Byers, "and then we'd send it back to our big 60,000-gallon tank. Production designer Naaman Marshall built a number of interior and exterior Kepler sets on soundstages, elevating them to allow for shaking and flooding effects. Even at slower speeds, we found if the velocity, gravity, intertia or deflection weren't quite right, the audience would feel it without being aware of it, and the integration would be lost. For some of the volumetric effects, the client wanted the mist to hang around longer than we initially anticipated, so the challenge was getting it to stay alive long enough without allowing it to appear to eject from a source. Since all the subsequent underwater scenes had been shot dry-for-wet, it fell to the UNDERWATER visual effects artists at MPC to make the characters' surrounding environment read as deep water. "William Eubank wanted the environment to look absolutely real," said MPC visual effects supervisor Axel Bonami, "so we based our shots of the characters walking underwater on reference of saturation diving. These are divers that dive down to 150 meters, in some cases, usually to do repairs on rigs, fixing pipes and such. There was a nice documentary about saturation diving on the BBC, and it included POV footage, looking out to the deep-water environment, and that gave us great reference. When you look at the recordings of these saturation divers, they are in a very murky, very dark environment." MPC began conducting tests on the dry-for-wet plates early in postproduction. Initially, the hope had been that many of the in-camera shots would suffice as is, with the pumped-in smoke creating enough of an underwater look, but close scrutiny of the plates revealed that, though dark and murky, they did not read as underwater environments. "As we looked at the footage," recalled Bonami, "everyone had the same comment: 'It doesn't look wet enough.' We realized quickly that we would have to alter the shading and lighting to give it an underwater look. The lighting was particularly important because light bounces off itself under water. It needed to look less specular and have more bounce. There needed to be less ambient light and more diffuse light. All of that is very difficult to get in a fully dry environment." The source of the lighting in what would otherwise be an all-black environment was the light coming from the characters' helmets, or illumination from the underwater drilling rigs.iAll of these light sources had to bounce 8 / 16 on the volume of water and on the silt to make it look right."

UNDERWATER MPC's visual effects crews, under CG supervisors Manolo Mantero and Nick Hamilton, wound up cheating the lighting in many instances as, in reality, light doesn't travel beyond 100 yards in deep water. "In order to see what was going on with the creatures and with the other characters," explained Bonami, "we couldn't have everything as dark and black as it would really be down there. We had scenes where you had to see something that was as much as a kilometer away; and so, we had to cheat the lighting somewhat." n addition to applying shaders and lighting tricks, MPC introduced movement into the underwater environments.iWe realized we had to add motions that people would recognize as underwater behaviors," Bonami said, "so we added slow, swirling motions, and introduced algae and other plant life that could move in that way to sell this as an underwater environment. Effects lead Francis Saint-Denis and his crew did a lot of effects simulations to create all the little floating particles, and we added wave motions. The magic trick that really sold it, we found, was adding little swirling bubbles in specific areas. That was a cheat, too, of course, because there wouldn't be any bubbles in the real world. Inner Demons BY GRAHAM EDWARDS very successful franchise has its spinoffs, and Marvel Comics' long-running X-Men series is no exception. Launched in 1982 by writer Chris Claremont and artist Bob McLeod, The New Mutants chronicles the adventures of a group of teenagers with genetically-driven superpowers. Boasting storylines rich in mysticism and oozing adolescent angst, the series became a favorite with fans of the already established XMen universe. The first big-screen adaptation of The New Mutants began life when writing partners Josh Boone and Knate Lee pitched a concept to producer Simon Kinberg. Appropriately enough, it was in the form of a comic book. "Knate is my best friend, who I've known basically since the day I was born," said Boone. "We grew up writing comic books together; we'd wanted to do something like this our whole lives. One thing we wanted was not to idealize the mutants' powers like they usually do in superhero movies. We wanted to make it more like Carrie or Firestarter, in terms of the powers being nightmares and curses to some degree. We pitched it as 'John Hughes meets Stephen King." 1 / 23 Boone and Lee drew inspiration from the 'Demon Bear' cycle of The New Mutants

THE NEW MUTANTS comics illustrated by Bill Sienkiewicz. In their script, young Danielle Moonstar (Blu Hunt) is haunted by dreams of a gigantic supernatural bear. At the climax of the film, she discovers that the bear casting a shadow across her life is the product of her own troubled psyche. "I had always loved Bill Sienkiewicz's run on The New Mutants," Boone asserted. "It was dark and interesting and character-driven. There was sexual tension and all sorts of things I hadn't read in X-Men comics before. Knate and I were really inspired by that and wanted to honor it. Bill himself came to the set, and we even had him illustrate some stuff for the credits sequence. The source material opened the door to a storyline rich in diversity. "It allowed us to do things that you don't typically do in movies. The main character, Dani, is a Native American girl. There's also a romance between Dani and Rahne. It's not made to be a big thing; they like each other and just happen to both be girls. You don't have to make the movie about a gay love story to have a couple be gay in it. First optioned by 20th Century Fox in 2015, The New Mutants embarked on principal photography in the summer of 2017, with Josh Boone at the helm.
